projects.title: Implement and Manage Virtual Networking
projects.summary: I extended my Azure network with a branch VNet and peering. I added NSGs, static IPs, a custom route table, a storage service endpoint, private DNS and a Standard Load Balancer.
projects.overview: In this project I extended an existing Azure network. I added a subnet and created a separate branch virtual network, then connected the two with peering in both directions. I configured security rules, static private and public IP addresses, a route table with my own routes, a service endpoint for Azure Storage and a private DNS zone linked to the network. I also deployed a Standard Load Balancer and enabled Network Watcher in East Asia. I checked the setup in the portal, Azure CLI and PowerShell.
objectives: Extend an existing network with a new subnet and a branch network.
Control traffic with NSG rules and custom routes.
Add private name resolution, a storage service endpoint and load balancing.
implementation: I created the extra subnet and the branch virtual network.
I set up peering between the main and branch networks in both directions.
I configured nsg-branch-1 with a rule that blocks RDP and a rule that allows HTTPS.
I set the static private IP 10.20.1.10 and added a Standard public IP.
I created the route table rt-branch-1 with a route that blocks 192.0.2.0/24 and attached it to snet-branch-1.
I enabled the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on the branch subnet.
I created the private DNS zone lab.inno.internal and linked it to the network.
I deployed the Standard Load Balancer lb-branch-1 with a TCP health probe and an HTTP rule on port 80.
verification: I confirmed the subnet ranges and the static private IP with Azure CLI and PowerShell.
Network Watcher showed as enabled in East Asia.

projects.title: Azure Subscription Governance
projects.summary: I used Azure Policy to make sure every resource carries an Environment tag. I also set up an Azure Automation runbook that shuts the VM down on a schedule to save cost.
projects.overview: Here I worked on governance and cost control in my Azure subscription. I assigned the built-in policy Require a tag on resources to my rg-rbac-lab resource group so that every resource must have the tag Environment=Lab. I then deployed an Ubuntu VM with its supporting resources and checked their compliance. Finally I created an Automation Account with a PowerShell runbook that shuts the VM down on a schedule.
objectives: Enforce a tagging rule on resources with Azure Policy.
Check compliance in the portal, Azure CLI and PowerShell.
Shut the VM down automatically on a schedule to control cost.
implementation: I reviewed my subscription details with Azure CLI queries and JSON output.
I assigned the tag policy to rg-rbac-lab requiring Environment=Lab.
I deployed an Ubuntu VM with its network interface, NSG, virtual network and disk.
I created the Automation Account aa-rbaclab-shutdown with a system-assigned managed identity. I gave the identity Virtual Machine Contributor on the VM only.
I published the Shutdown-VM-Daily-UAE runbook with three daily schedules at 2:00 AM, 5:00 PM and 10:00 PM UAE time.
verification: Compliance showed all five resources as compliant in the portal, Azure CLI and PowerShell.
A runbook job completed and PowerShell showed the VM as deallocated.

projects.title: Network Automation with Python and Netmiko
projects.status: In progress. The Python stage is published and the later stages are still to come.
projects.summary: My Python scripts connect to a Cisco router with Netmiko, read the device information, tidy it with TextFSM and save a JSON report.
projects.overview: I wrote Python scripts that log in to a Cisco IOS router (R1) with Netmiko, run show version and show ip interface brief, turn the interface table into structured data with TextFSM and save it as a JSON report. My later version reads the device details from a JSON inventory file. The repository lists more stages I plan to add, such as Ansible and NETCONF. So far only the Python stage is published.
objectives: Collect device information automatically instead of typing commands by hand.
Read the devices from an inventory file instead of hard-coding them.
implementation: device_info.py connects to R1, runs the show commands and picks out the hostname, IOS version, uptime and interfaces.
inventory_reader.py and inventory_connection.py read inventory/devices.json and open a Netmiko session.
collect_device_info.py puts both together and writes api/<hostname>-device-info.json.
verification: My screenshots show the Netmiko connection to R1 and the structured output.
The report api/r1-device-info.json shows IOS 17.15.1 and four interfaces with their status.

projects.title: Enterprise Compute and Application Infrastructure
projects.summary: I set up an Ubuntu 24.04 server in Azure with no public IP. It reaches the internet through a NAT Gateway and I manage it through Azure Bastion. It runs a Flask web portal on Gunicorn with a PostgreSQL 16 database in Docker.
projects.overview: In this project I built a small internal business application environment in Azure. I deployed an Ubuntu Server 24.04 virtual machine without a public IP address. I configured the application subnet and its security rules, gave the subnet outbound internet access through an Azure NAT Gateway and used Azure Bastion to open the server desktop safely from the portal. On the server I installed Docker and Docker Compose, ran PostgreSQL 16 as the database and deployed my Enterprise Management Portal, a Flask application served by Gunicorn.
objectives: Host an internal application on a server that has no public IP address.
Give the server controlled outbound access and safe admin access.
Run the database in containers and connect a Python web application to it.
implementation: I created the application subnet and its network security group.
I deployed the Ubuntu Server 24.04 virtual machine and checked the operating system.
I created a static public IP and a NAT Gateway for the subnet's outbound traffic.
I opened the Ubuntu desktop through Azure Bastion.
I deployed PostgreSQL 16 with Docker Compose and created the enterprise_portal database with its own application account.
I deployed the Flask portal behind Gunicorn.
verification: I checked the application health endpoint, the database connection and the Gunicorn service.
I opened the portal dashboard in Firefox on the server at 127.0.0.1:8080.
I reviewed the final inbound security rules for SSH, internal HTTPS and Bastion access.
